vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/nan-bare-is-a-number-token-not-a-label
vectors.comment: `nan` is claimed by the reserved-float-spelling tokenizer rule (rule 7) before IDENT is reached, so it never reaches label position at all and is not the reserved-word-label error nan/inf never get. But it is not a token-level mismatch either, which is what this vector claimed while expecting parse.unexpected-token until v0.19.0-beta: the parser takes the scalar branch, consumes `nan` as a NUMBER, and then fails on the leftover `:` exactly as `null: 1` does. Sec4.6.1's OML-25 now states the general rule -- any scalar followed by leftover content at document level is parse.trailing-content, at the first leftover token. `nan: 1` is 3 characters then the colon, so 1:4. Whether the tokenizer or the parser excluded the word from label position is spent before the scalar branch is taken and does not change the code. The reference emits parse.unexpected-token at 1:4 (code wrong, position right); recorded as DIV-4.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/inf-bare-is-a-number-token-not-a-label
vectors.comment: OML-25's companion to the `nan` vector: `inf` is claimed by the same reserved-float-spelling tokenizer rule, takes the same scalar branch, and fails the same way. `inf` is 3 characters, so the leftover colon is at 1:4. The reference emits parse.unexpected-token at 1:4 (DIV-4).

vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/bare-integer-then-colon-is-trailing-content
vectors.comment: OML-25 with no reserved word involved at all: an INTEGER is a scalar, the top-level lookahead (Sec4.6.1) only routes a STRING or a non-reserved IDENT to the edge branch, so `5` is consumed as the document's single scalar and the `:` is leftover. `5` is one character, so the colon is at 1:2. This is the vector that shows the rule is about scalar-then-leftover generally and not about `null`/`nan`/`inf` specifically. The reference emits parse.unexpected-token at 1:2 (DIV-4).

vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/quoted-nan-is-an-ordinary-label
vectors.comment: Quoting routes `nan` to the STRING tokenizer rule (rule 1) instead of the reserved float spelling, so it is a perfectly ordinary label here.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/null-bare-label-at-top-level-fails-on-trailing-colon
vectors.comment: The sharp edge in Sec4.6.1: `null` fails the edge-vs-scalar lookahead test (it IS null/true/false), so the parser takes the scalar branch, consumes `null`, and then fails on the leftover `:` as trailing content -- NOT the reserved-word-label error. Distinguishing these two by code is exactly what Sec4.6.1 says conformance vectors must do.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/null-bare-label-inside-a-node-is-the-reserved-word-error
vectors.comment: Inside a node, label position is unambiguous (no top-level scalar-or-edge lookahead applies), so this is the specific reserved-word-label error rather than a trailing-content error -- the companion case to the top-level vector above.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/arrays/repeated-label-sugar-expands-in-place
vectors.comment: [1,2,3] expands at parse time into three repeated `b` edges -- indistinguishable from writing `b: 1; b: 2; b: 3` directly. An array is not a value in the Document model.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/arrays/empty-array-is-an-error-not-a-zero-edge-expansion
vectors.comment: An empty array and an absent label are the same Document, and OML deliberately does not offer two spellings for one thing.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/arrays/nested-array-is-rejected
vectors.comment: An array element that is itself an array has nothing to nest into -- the Document model has no bare nested list (Sec2.2.3).

vectors.name: oml-grammar/arrays/newline-inside-array-is-an-error
vectors.comment: Comma is the only element separator inside [...]. A newline immediately after a real comma is legal and purely decorative (Sec4.3.1's fourth rule: separators and comments are otherwise insignificant inside [...]) -- this vector's original input mistakenly had a comma present ("b: [1,\n2, 3]\n"), which never exercised the illegal case its name claimed and was correctly flagged by the omnist-py session (omnist#284, closed not-a-bug) before implementation. This corrected input has NO comma between 1 and 2, so the newline is the only thing standing in for a separator, which is exactly the illegal case. Confirmed live: fails at line 2, col 1 with 'expected , or ] in array'.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/strings/raw-string-performs-no-escape-processing
vectors.comment: Raw strings (Extended, read-only) perform no escape processing at all -- a backslash inside is a literal backslash, unlike the double-quoted Core form.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/strings/multiline-string-strips-leading-newline
vectors.comment: The optional newline immediately after the opening """ is consumed and is not part of the value.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/strings/multiline-string-closes-at-first-run-of-three-quotes
vectors.comment: A run of one or two quotes inside a multiline string is literal content; the string only closes at a run of three or more, and only the first three of that run are consumed as the terminator.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/date-then-time-lookahead-yields-one-datetime-token
vectors.comment: At a position where DATE matches, the tokenizer checks whether the next character is T followed by a TIME-shaped lookahead; here it is, so DATETIME is emitted as one token rather than DATE followed by a separate value.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/date-then-non-time-suffix-is-date-plus-trailing-content
vectors.comment: The lookahead after DATE fails (T99 does not match TIME), so DATE is emitted alone and whatever follows -- the bare identifier T99 -- is tokenized independently, then rejected as trailing content once the single-value position is already filled.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/shape/single-top-level-scalar-is-the-whole-document
vectors.comment: One of the three legal top-level shapes: the document IS that one leaf, with no wrapper.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/errors/bare-word-in-value-position-is-an-error
vectors.comment: A bare identifier that is not null/true/false is not a string -- OML has no implicit string-from-identifier coercion anywhere.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/errors/literal-control-character-in-string-is-an-error
vectors.comment: A literal control character below U+0020 -- here a raw newline before the closing quote -- is an error in a double-quoted (Core) string.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/errors/unrecognized-escape-is-an-error
vectors.comment: Recognized escapes are exactly \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t and \uXXXX; \q is none of these.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/errors/unpaired-high-surrogate-is-an-error
vectors.comment: A \uXXXX in the high-surrogate range D800-DBFF MUST be immediately followed by a second \uXXXX in the low-surrogate range DC00-DFFF; this one has no partner.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/errors/unterminated-string-is-an-error
vectors.comment: End of input reached with the string still open -- no closing quote.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/numbers/leading-zero-integer-is-an-error
vectors.comment: int-part only permits a single 0, or a nonzero digit followed by more digits -- never a 0 followed by more digits. This closes previously-undefined behavior: nothing in this spec constrained NUMBER/INTEGER lexically before Sec4.2.3 existed.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/numbers/leading-zero-in-decimal-is-an-error
vectors.comment: The leading-zero restriction on int-part applies identically whether the literal ends up tokenized as INTEGER or NUMBER -- a fractional part does not exempt the integer part from the same rule.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/numbers/single-zero-and-negative-forms-are-valid
vectors.comment: A bare 0 is exactly one digit, so it's never a leading zero; a fraction less than 1 legitimately starts with 0.; a negative sign does not change int-part's own leading-zero rule since it applies after the optional minus.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/date-with-out-of-range-month-is-an-error
vectors.comment: ABNF's 2DIGIT for the month component permits 00-99; only 01-12 are calendar-valid, and that range check is normative even though ABNF cannot express it.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/date-with-day-invalid-for-month-is-an-error
vectors.comment: February never has a 30th day regardless of leap year, distinguishing this from the leap-year-specific case below.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/february-29-in-a-non-leap-year-is-an-error
vectors.comment: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not 400, so it is not a leap year in the proleptic Gregorian calendar -- distinct from 2000-02-29 (the happy-path vector below), which is.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/february-29-in-a-leap-year-is-valid
vectors.comment: 2000 is divisible by 400, so it is a leap year -- the one case the div-by-100 exception itself has an exception for.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/leap-second-is-an-error
vectors.comment: OML has no leap-second spelling; second is 00-59 with no exception, unlike ISO 8601 which permits 60 in some contexts.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/tz-offset-minute-out-of-range-is-an-error
vectors.comment: tz-offset MUST use the same minute range as TIME (00-59), not a wider one. This is the case that surfaced the gap: an implementation that validates tz-offset via a separate code path from TIME can end up normalizing +00:60 to a 1-hour offset instead of rejecting it, silently colliding it with a document that legitimately wrote +01:00 -- confirmed live against a pre-fix reference implementation. The offset MUST be rejected outright, not normalized.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/temporals/tz-offset-within-range-is-valid
vectors.comment: A legitimate, in-range offset (e.g. India Standard Time) parses normally -- confirms the tz-offset fix in the vector above doesn't reject valid input, only out-of-range minutes. The expected value's seconds are canonicalized to :00 even though the source text omits them, matching every sibling OML-datetime vector's own convention (see date-then-time-lookahead-yields-one-datetime-token above) -- a temporal-scalar value in a parse vector MUST already be in the format's own canonical spelling, not just any value that happens to compare semantically equal, since a string-backed implementation (rather than one with a native temporal type) compares literally. Was originally un-canonicalized here; found and reported as omnist-spec#51 by the Rust port during omnist-rs#165.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/encoding/leading-bom-is-stripped
vectors.comment: Sec2.5: a byte-order mark at the very start of input is consumed and contributes nothing to the Document -- the result is identical to the same input without it. Stripping rather than rejecting is deliberate: BOM-prefixed files are routine from Windows tooling, and refusing them would reject well-formed data over a byte the author never sees. A BOM anywhere other than position zero is ordinary content with no special meaning.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/encoding/nfc-and-nfd-labels-are-distinct
vectors.comment: Sec2.5: labels compare byte-wise, never by Unicode normalization. Both labels render as 'cafe-acute' but differ in bytes -- one is U+00E9, the other 'e' followed by combining U+0301 -- so they are two distinct labels and the node has two edges. An implementation that normalizes to NFC or NFD on read collapses them into one edge and fails here. This is the rule most likely to be broken by accident, since some platforms normalize text input by default.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/encoding/doubled-leading-bom-is-rejected
vectors.comment: D-21: D-15 consumes exactly one leading U+FEFF and stops, and a reader MUST then reject a second mark still standing at offset zero of what remains. That is a rule Omnist imposes, not one read off each format -- the formats disagree, and this vector's own note below says what this one would do unaided. The position is 1:1 because it is computed on the text remaining after the strip, not on the original input. OML is one of the three surfaces where the rule costs nothing: grammars/oml.abnf admits BOM at offset zero and nowhere else, so a second mark is already a syntax error on OML's own terms. Companion to oml-grammar/encoding/leading-bom-is-stripped, the same input with one mark. Measured: the reference already rejects this with parse.unexpected-token at 1:1 -- green on arrival.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/errors/newline-separated-second-scalar-is-trailing-content
vectors.comment: OML-25's position rule with no reserved word and no colon involved: `1` is the document's single scalar and `2` is leftover. The position is the first leftover **significant** token -- the `2` at 2:1 -- not the separator in front of it, which Sec4.2.1 collapses and which would be 1:2. Counted from the input: line 1 is `1`, line 2 is `2` at column 1. The reference reports the right position here and the wrong code, parse.unexpected-token (DIV-4).

vectors.name: oml-grammar/comments/trailing-comment-after-a-lone-scalar-is-not-trailing-content
vectors.comment: The companion to the vector above, pinning what 'leftover' excludes. Sec4.2.1 skips comments at tokenization, so a comment emits no token and cannot be leftover content: `1 # done` is the valid single-scalar document 1. Without this vector OML-25's 'first leftover significant token' has nothing holding the word significant to Sec4.2.1's meaning, and an implementation that reported trailing content here would look defensible. Confirmed live against the reference, which accepts it and returns the scalar 1.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/reserved/true-bare-label-at-top-level-fails-on-trailing-colon
vectors.comment: The fifth member of OML-25's list, which enumerates null/true/nan/inf/5 and until now had a vector for every one of them except `true`. `true` is an IDENT excluded from label position by the parser, exactly like `null`, so the lookahead declines the edge branch, the scalar is consumed and the `:` is leftover. `true` is 4 characters, so the colon is at 1:5. The reference emits parse.unexpected-token at 1:5 -- position right, code wrong (DIV-4).

vectors.name: oml-grammar/shape/missing-separator-after-top-level-edge-is-trailing-content
vectors.comment: OML-26. The edge `a: 1` is complete, and a complete top-level edge can end the document (Sec4.6's second legal shape), so the `b` standing there with no separator is content after the document ended -- parse.trailing-content, at the first leftover significant token. Counting: a(1) :(2) space(3) 1(4) space(5) b(6), so 1:6. Measured live against the Python reference: parse.unexpected-token at 1:6 -- position right, code wrong, recorded as DIV-4. TypeScript, Go and Rust implement OML-26 per their v0.19.0-beta sweeps and are expected to pass; Java has not been measured against this rule and is not claimed (DIV-4).

vectors.name: oml-grammar/shape/missing-separator-inside-a-node-is-an-unexpected-token
vectors.comment: OML-27, the other side of OML-26 and the reason it is scoped to top level: inside `{...}` a closing brace is still owed, so the identical missing separator is a token where the grammar does not allow one rather than content after a finished document. Counting: a(1) :(2) sp(3) {(4) sp(5) b(6) :(7) sp(8) 1(9) sp(10) c(11), so 1:11. Measured live against the Python reference: parse.unexpected-token at 1:11 -- agrees on both code and position.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/arrays/missing-comma-between-elements-is-an-unexpected-token
vectors.comment: OML-27 inside brackets. Sec4.3.1 makes the comma the only element separator, so after `1` the grammar owes a `,` or a `]` and the `2` is neither. Not parse.separator-in-array, which Sec8.3.1 reserves for a newline or `;` used as an array separator -- there is no separator here at all. Not parse.trailing-content either: the `]` is still owed, so nothing has ended. Counting: a(1) :(2) sp(3) [(4) 1(5) sp(6) 2(7), so 1:7. Measured live against the Python reference: parse.unexpected-token at 1:7 -- agrees on both code and position.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/shape/stray-closing-brace-after-a-top-level-edge-is-trailing-content
vectors.comment: OML-26 holds whatever the leftover token is, including one that could not begin a document: no document starts with `}`. Nothing is owed at top level -- OML-27 turns on an unclosed `{` or `[` and there is none here -- so the document body is complete and the `}` is content after it. Counting: a(1) :(2) sp(3) 1(4) sp(5) }(6), so 1:6. Measured live against the Python reference: parse.unexpected-token at 1:6, and its own message reads "unexpected trailing content after the document body (token RBRACE '}')" -- it already calls this trailing content and reports the other code. Position right, code wrong; recorded as DIV-4.

vectors.name: oml-grammar/shape/stray-comma-after-a-top-level-edge-is-trailing-content
vectors.comment: The sibling of the stray-closing-brace vector, for the other token that cannot begin a document. A comma is an element separator inside `[...]` (Sec4.3.1) and has no top-level role at all, but OML-26 does not branch on what the leftover token could have meant -- the body is complete and the comma is after it. Counting: a(1) :(2) sp(3) 1(4) sp(5) ,(6), so 1:6. Measured live against the Python reference: parse.unexpected-token at 1:6 -- position right, code wrong; recorded as DIV-4.
